extraction.name: SWE-Gym
extraction.description: A training environment containing 2,438 real-world software engineering tasks from 11 popular open-source Python repositories. Each task includes a natural-language issue description, a codebase snapshot, a pre-configured executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a human-submitted solution patch. SWE-Gym Lite contains 230 easier, more self-contained tasks. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 instances from 358 Python repositories without executable environments.
extraction.creator: Jiayi Pan; Xingyao Wang; Graham Neubig; Navdeep Jaitly; Heng Ji; Alane Suhr; Yizhe Zhang
extraction.citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, and Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025. arXiv:2412.21139v2.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Repositories were identified using SEART GitHub search. The authors selected Python repositories created before July 1, 2022, with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and at least 100 contributors, yielding 358 repositories. SWE-Bench's instance extraction script produced 64,689 task instances. The authors then focused on 11 repositories with numerous instances, semi-automatically associated instances with software versions, manually configured dependencies, and validated instances through execution. After filtering failed instances, 2,438 tasks remained. Environment construction required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Software Collection; Manual Human Curator; User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: SWE-Gym Raw instances contain code, issue descriptions, and solutions, but lack executable environments and a guarantee that their unit tests effectively evaluate solution correctness. During one GPT-4o trajectory-sampling run, infrastructure-related errors caused some instances to fail to complete, so the reported successful-trajectory count may underestimate the actual count.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world GitHub issues and associated pull requests from open-source Python repositories, including natural-language issue descriptions, repository snapshots, human-submitted code patches, and unit tests. The final repositories are pandas, MONAI, moto, mypy, dvc, dask, modin, pydantic, conan, hydra, and bokeh.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Instances were associated with software version numbers using a generalized SWE-Bench versioning script and repository information such as pyproject.toml files and git tags. For trajectory-training experiments, the authors selected successful trajectories through rejection sampling. MoatlessTools training capped successful trajectories at two per task, preferring trajectories with fewer model response rounds. Verifier datasets balanced successful and unsuccessful trajectories through subsampling. Scaling experiments also deduplicated trajectories by instance ID and sampled subsets randomly or by repository.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Dependencies were manually configured using configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at issue creation. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script checked that the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code; failed instances were removed. SWE-Gym Lite followed the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring edits to more than one file, poorly described problem statements, excessively complex ground-truth diffs, and tests focused on error-message validation. OpenHands verifier training retained only trajectories within 32,000 tokens. MoatlessTools verifier inputs combined task descriptions, relevant context extracted from agent trajectories, and generated patches.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human developers supplied the original issue descriptions, solution patches, and test suites. A subset of the paper's authors manually configured task dependencies and performed environment-construction annotations, totaling approximately 200 hours. Gold patches were validated using executable unit tests. Sampled agent trajectories were labeled successful or unsuccessful using SWE-Gym test suites. OpenHands verifier training represented these outcomes as YES or NO judgments; the MoatlessTools verifier prompt used True or False.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Execution-based validation required the human-submitted gold patch to pass more unit tests than the original code. Instances failing validation were filtered out. Trajectory success labels were determined using the included test suites.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench execution-based validation script; SWE-Gym executable unit-test suites.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Improved software engineering agents could increase developer productivity, support critical open-source infrastructure, and make software development more accessible. More capable agents may affect software engineering jobs and raise concerns about code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could be misused to automate malicious-code creation. The authors encourage responsible-deployment frameworks addressing security, safety, and economic impacts.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Tasks have a long-tail distribution across repositories: pandas accounts for nearly one-third of instances, while bokeh accounts for approximately one percent. Rejection sampling produces a bias toward easier tasks because those tasks generate more successful trajectories; per-instance capping was used to mitigate this bias. The authors manually configured environments to avoid potential distribution bias from excluding tasks with complex dependencies. SWE-Gym repositories are separate from SWE-Bench repositories to avoid contamination.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Environment diversity is limited in repository count, task types, and programming languages. SWE-Gym Raw lacks executable environments and guarantees of effective unit-test evaluation. SWE-Gym tasks appear harder on average than SWE-Bench tasks, with larger gold patches and consistently lower model performance. Current software engineering settings focus on task completion rather than human-in-the-loop collaboration. The models presented are research artifacts and are not yet production-ready.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training and supervised fine-tuning of software engineering agents; rejection-sampling self-improvement; training outcome-supervised verifier models from successful and unsuccessful agent trajectories; studying training-time and inference-time scaling. SWE-Gym Lite supports rapid prototyping and faster agent evaluation. SWE-Gym Raw supports future software engineering agent research and automatic dataset synthesis.
